summary: Describes how an AAA server such as RADIUS or Diameter can help a Mobile IPv4 node and its home agent set up the strong authentication they need, using the security association the node already shares with its home AAA server.

plainLanguage.summary: Mobile IPv4 needs strong authentication between the mobile node and its home agent, and a node that has just arrived in a new network may hold no key for either agent. This RFC lets an AAA server supply key material through the registration exchange, so the node can derive the keys it needs from the one key it already shares with its home AAA server.

questions: how does mobile ipv4 get keys from aaa
what is a key generation nonce
what is a mobility security association
subtitle: How an AAA server can hand a mobile node the keys it needs with its home and foreign agents.

tldr.problem: Mobile IP for IPv4 requires strong authentication between the mobile node and its home agent, and a node that has just arrived in a foreign network may hold no key for either agent.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds four extensions to Mobile IP registration messages. The mobile node asks for key material in its registration request, the AAA server generates a random Key Generation Nonce, and the node derives the keys it needs from that nonce and the AAA key it already shares with its home AAA server.
tldr.outcome: The node can create a Mobility Security Association with its home agent and foreign agent without a separate key exchange with either of them. The RFC states that these keys are no stronger than the AAA security association they come from, so that association must be refreshed periodically.

facts.label: Extension types
facts.value: 40 MN-FA KeyGen Request, 41 MN-FA KeyGen Reply, 42 MN-HA KeyGen Request, 43 MN-HA KeyGen Reply

facts.label: Key Generation Nonce size
facts.value: A random value of at least 128 bits

facts.label: Replay methods used
facts.value: 2 Timestamps and 3 Nonces; 0 and 1 reserved, 4 to 65535 unallocated

today: RFC 3957 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2005, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the extension to Mobile IPv4 registration messages that lets an AAA server supply key material to a mobile node.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
AAA servers, such as RADIUS and DIAMETER, are in use within the Internet today to provide authentication and authorization services for dial-up computers. Such services are likely to be valuable for mobile nodes using Mobile IP for IPv4, when the nodes are attempting to connect to foreign domains with AAA servers. Requirements for interactions between AAA and Mobile IP are outlined in RFC 2977, which describes an infrastructure that enables AAA servers to authenticate and authorize network access requests from mobile nodes. The Mobile IP Registration Request is considered to be a request for network access, and it is possible to augment the mobility agents so that they can translate between Mobile IP registration messages and the messages used within the AAA infrastructure.

This specification makes use of a single AAA Security Association to create derivative Mobility Security Associations. A Mobility Security Association here is a simplex connection that serves to authenticate Mobile IPv4 control traffic between a mobile node and its home agent and, or, its foreign agent. It is identified by the two end points and an SPI.

AAA servers typically use the Network Access Identifier to uniquely identify the mobile node, so a mobile node can authenticate itself and be authorized for connection to the foreign domain without having any home address. For Mobile IP to work, however, the node is required to have a home address and a Mobility Security Association with its home agent. When the Registration Reply is authenticated by the MN-AAA Authentication Extension, the mobile node can verify that the key material in the extensions was produced by the AAA server, and can then rely on it to create the associations with the home agent and, or, the foreign agent.
sections.plainLanguage: A mobile node that travels to another network has to register there, and it must prove who it is to both the foreign agent and its home agent. Many operators already run AAA servers for dial-up access. This RFC reuses the key the node already has with its home AAA server to make the keys it needs with the two agents.

sections.title: The Terms the RFC Defines
sections.content:
An AAA entity is a network node processing AAA messages. An AAA Security Association is a security association between an AAA entity and another node that needs the services of that AAA entity; in this document all of them are between a mobile node and its home AAA server, and the key is referred to as the AAA-key. It may be based on the mobile node's IP address or on its Network Access Identifier.

A Mobility Security Association is a simplex connection that applies security services to Mobile IPv4 control traffic between a mobile node and a home agent, or a mobile node and a foreign agent, using the Mobile IP Authentication Extensions. It is uniquely identified by the peer source and destination IP addresses and an SPI.

A Key Generation Nonce is nonce data used for the purpose of creating a key. A Registration Key is a key used in the MN-FA or MN-HA Mobility Security Association, typically used only once or a very few times, and only for verifying a small volume of authentication data. A Key is a number kept secret. A Security Algorithm is a set of rules for using input data and a secret key to produce data for use in security protocols. The SPI, Security Parameters Index, is an arbitrary 32-bit value that assists in identifying an AAA, IP or Mobility Security Association.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC names three things. The AAA Security Association is the shared secret between the node and its home AAA server. A Mobility Security Association is a one-way protected link between the node and one agent, identified by the two addresses and a security parameters index. A Key Generation Nonce is a random value the AAA server sends so the node can derive a key from the AAA key.

sections.title: The Exchange, Step by Step
sections.content:
When a mobile node depends on an AAA infrastructure for authorization and Mobile IP registration, it may lack any pre-existing Mobility Security Association with either its home agent or the foreign agent. The key material may be requested by the mobile node in new extensions to Mobile IP Registration Request messages and supplied to the mobile node in extensions to the Registration Reply. Alternatively the AAA server MAY provide unsolicited key material via mobility agents, in which case the mobile node MUST then calculate new keys and update or create its relevant Mobility Security Association.

  1. If the mobile node does not have a Mobility Security Association with the foreign agent, it SHOULD include an MN-FA Key Generation Nonce Request extension in its Registration Request.
  2. If it does not have one with the home agent, it MUST add an MN-HA Key Generation Nonce Request extension.
  3. If one or more of those extensions were added, the mobile node MUST add the MN-AAA Authentication extension.
  4. The foreign agent, which is presumed to be also an AAA entity, transfers the key requests and authentication data to the local AAA server.
  5. After the information in the MN-AAA Authentication extension is verified by the AAA server in the home domain, it generates the key material that was requested.
  6. The respective keys for the Mobility Security Associations are distributed to the home agent and foreign agent via the AAA protocol.
  7. The mobile node receives the Registration Reply message from the foreign agent.
  8. If an MN-HA Key Generation Nonce From AAA extension is present, the mobile node MUST create or update its Mobility Security Association with the home agent using the key computed from that extension. If no MN-HA Key Generation Nonce Reply extension is present, the mobile node MUST discard the Registration Reply.
  9. Using its new association with the home agent, the mobile node authenticates the Registration Reply by checking the Authentication Data in the Mobile-Home Authentication extension. If the check fails, it MUST discard the reply and the new association, reverting to the old one if any.
  10. If the reply passes authentication and contains an MN-FA Key Generation Nonce From AAA extension, the mobile node generates the registration key from the nonce and its AAA Security Association, and uses it to establish its Mobility Security Association with the foreign agent and to compute the authentication data used in the Mobile-Foreign authentication extension.
sections.plainLanguage: The node asks for key material inside its registration request. The foreign agent passes the request to the local AAA server, and the home AAA server checks the node's authentication data before generating the key material. The keys reach the two agents over the AAA protocol, and the reply carries the random value back to the node. The node then derives its keys and checks the home agent's authentication data. If that check fails, the node throws the reply away and keeps the association it had before.

sections.title: What a Mobility Security Association Holds
sections.content:
Mobility Security Associations between Mobile IP entities contain both the necessary cryptographic key information and a way to identify the cryptographic transform that uses the key to produce the authentication information present in the Mobile-Home Authentication extension or the Mobile-Foreign Authentication extension. In order for the mobile node to make use of key material created by the AAA server, it also has to be able to identify and select the appropriate cryptographic transform that uses the key to produce the authentication.

The transform identifiers are the same as those used in IPsec. They are tabulated in the list of Authentication Algorithms allowable as values for the Attribute Type 5, the Authentication Algorithm, one of the classifications in the tabulated Attribute Types for IPsec Security Association Attributes.

Mobility Security Associations shared between mobile nodes and home agents also require a replay protection method. The supported replay detection methods are listed in the RFC: values 0 and 1 are reserved, 2 is Timestamps as defined in RFC 3344, 3 is Nonces as defined in RFC 3344, and 4 to 65535 are unallocated.
sections.plainLanguage: A Mobility Security Association holds two things: the key, and the name of the transform that turns that key into authentication data. The transform names come from the IPsec list. Associations between a node and its home agent also need a replay protection method, and the RFC allows two: timestamps and nonces.

sections.title: Creating the Nonce and Deriving the Key
sections.content:
This section contains the procedures followed in the creation of the Key Generation Nonce by AAA servers and the key derivation procedures used by mobile nodes. The AAA servers also deliver the keys to the mobility agents, the home agent and the foreign agent, via the AAA protocol. The mobility agents faithfully transcribe the results into the appropriate Mobile IP extensions.

The example uses HMAC-SHA1. All mobile nodes and mobility agents implementing Mobile IP and implementing the extensions specified in this document MUST implement HMAC-SHA1. Other message authentication codes or keyed hash functions MAY also be used, and the particular algorithm used is configured as part of the AAA Security Association between the mobile node and the AAAH server, which is in turn indexed by the AAA SPI.

The steps performed on the AAAH server are: the AAA server identifies the mobile node, using the NAI field if it is present in the Registration Request and otherwise the Home Address field; it generates a random value of at least 128 bits to be used as the Key Generation Nonce; and it inserts that value into the Key Generation Nonce Reply extension in the Key Generation Nonce field.

The mobile node then calculates the key, where the double bar represents concatenation:

key = HMAC-SHA1 (AAA-key, {Key Generation Nonce || mobile node identifier})

The Key Generation Nonce is the one from the extension in the Registration Reply, and the mobile node identifier is the node's NAI if present in the Registration Request or the Home Address otherwise. The mobile node then creates the Mobility Security Associations, using the resulting key and the other relevant information in the Key Generation Nonce Extension. The secret key used inside the HMAC-SHA1 computation is the one in the AAA Security Association indexed by the AAA SPI.
sections.plainLanguage: The AAA server picks a random value of at least 128 bits and puts it in the reply. The node then computes its key by running HMAC-SHA1 over the AAA key and the random value joined to the node's identifier. HMAC-SHA1 is the one algorithm every implementation must support; others are allowed and are chosen when the AAA association is set up.

sections.title: The Four New Registration Extensions
sections.content:
Four new extensions are defined for Mobile IP Registration Requests and Replies. Each has a Type, a Subtype, a 16-bit Length and subtype-specific data.

  • Type 40, not skippable, is the Generalized MN-FA Key Generation Nonce Request extension. It carries the Mobile Node SPI that the mobile node will assign for the Mobility Security Association created for use with the registration key. Its Length equals the number of bytes in the subtype data plus 4, for the SPI field.
  • Type 41, not skippable, is the Generalized MN-FA Key Generation Nonce Reply extension, which supplies the keying material. Its subtype 1 carries a Lifetime in seconds, a 32-bit AAA SPI, the FA SPI, an Algorithm Identifier and the Key Generation Nonce, a random value of at least 128 bits. It MUST appear in the Registration Reply before the Mobile-Foreign Authentication extension.
  • Type 42, not skippable, is the Generalized MN-HA Key Generation Nonce Request extension, with the same Mobile Node SPI layout.
  • Type 43, not skippable, is the Generalized MN-HA Key Generation Nonce Reply extension. Its subtype 1 carries a Lifetime in seconds and then the AAA SPI, the HA SPI, an Algorithm Identifier, a Replay Method and the Key Generation Nonce. It MUST appear in the Registration Reply before the MN-HA Authentication extension.

Subtype 1 of each of the four is the version that takes the key material from the AAA server. The two request extensions have a zero-length Subtype Data field and MUST appear in the Registration Request before the MN-AAA Authentication extension. A Registration Reply that carries an MN-HA Key Generation Nonce From AAA extension MUST also carry a subsequent Mobile Home Authentication extension, created using the generated MN-HA key; the same holds for the MN-FA case and the Mobile Foreign Authentication extension.

If the foreign agent receives a Registration Reply with no MN-FA Key Generation Nonce Reply extension, and has no existing Mobility Security Association with the mobile node, it MAY change the Code value of the reply to MISSING_MN_FA, which has the value 107, effectively causing the registration to fail. IANA keeps a registry of KeyGen Request and Reply subtypes, whose initial content is the single entry for the subtypes defined here, with value 1. A separate namespace exists for the Replay Method Identifier, of which this specification uses 2 and 3.
sections.plainLanguage: Four new extensions carry the request and the reply. The request extensions have numbers 40 and 42, and the reply extensions 41 and 43. Each has a subtype, and subtype 1 in each means the key material comes from the AAA server. The reply for the home agent also carries the lifetime of the key, the algorithm to use and the replay method to use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions in this document are intended to provide the appropriate level of security for Mobile IP entities to calculate the Authentication Data needed by the authentication extensions used with Mobile IP registration messages. The Mobility Security Associations resulting from the use of these extensions do not offer any higher level of security than what is already implicit in the use of the AAA Security Association between the mobile node and the AAAH. In order to deny any adversary the luxury of unbounded time to analyze and break the secrecy of that AAA Security Association, it MUST be refreshed periodically. The provisioning and refreshing of the AAA key in the mobile node and the AAA server is outside the scope of this document.

Since the Reply extensions defined in this specification only carry Key Generation Nonces, which are used to derive keys, they do not expose any data that could be used in an attack aimed at recovering the key shared between the mobile node and the AAA. The authors do not believe this specification introduces any new security vulnerability.
sections.plainLanguage: The keys this scheme produces are no stronger than the AAA association they come from, so that association has to be renewed on a schedule so that an attacker cannot spend unlimited time on it. The reply extensions carry only the random nonces, not the derived keys, so they do not expose anything that would help recover the AAA key.
